title: Mudarabah: A Teacher's Manual
subtitle: From the first definition to the governance rules. Master course, edition 7 (2026).
One of the core contracts of Islamic finance.

blocks.x: How to use this manual

**Who it is for.** A teacher who will explain mudarabah to people who work in finance but know no Arabic and nothing of Islamic law. The manual assumes no prior knowledge. Every Arabic word is explained the first time it appears and is listed in the glossary (Part 8).
**How it is built.** Eight parts, each building on the last:

i: The word and the idea
Mudarabah in academic terms: what kind of contract it is, and why it is allowed
The rules, with every school's position
Mudarabah in practice: how it is used today
Governance: what the six regulatory frameworks require
Teaching aids: worked cases, review questions, common mistakes
The scholars and works quoted
Glossary

blocks.x: **How sources are shown.** Every rule carries its source in brackets: the author and the page, or the standard and the clause. For example "(Usmani, p. 34)" or "(AAOIFI SS 13, 4/4)". **Hadith** (reports of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did or approved) are cited by collection and report number. Quotations from the Muwatta of Malik and from al-Kafi are from English translations. Where a report's grade is given, it is the grade in the edition used, unless a grader is named. Quotations from Arabic books with no English edition named are this manual's own translations. Where the scholars or schools disagree, every view is given with the name of the person or school who holds it. No view is presented as "the" answer. Where an author gives his own opinion, it is marked as his.

**Words used throughout.** *Shari'ah* is Islamic law as a whole; *fiqh* is that law as the jurists work it out. The *Sunnah* is the Prophet's example, known through hadith. The *Companions* are the people who knew the Prophet and followed him. A *caliph* is a leader of the Muslim community after the Prophet; Umar and Uthman, named below, were the second and third caliphs. *Sunni* and *Shia* are the two main branches of Islam. In the Shia branch, an *Imam* is one of the leaders from the Prophet's family whose reports carry authority. Among Sunnis, *Imam* is also a title of respect for a leading scholar, as in "Imam Malik" or "Imam Ahmad". A *dirham* was a silver coin and a *dinar* a gold coin; the classical books state cash amounts in them. Dates are given in the common era (CE) unless marked **AH**: years of the Islamic lunar calendar, counted from the Prophet's emigration to Medina in 622 CE.

**The schools named in this manual.** Islamic law has several schools (in Arabic *madhhab*, plural *madhahib*). Four are Sunni and are named after early jurists: the **Hanafi** (Abu Hanifah, d. 767), **Maliki** (Malik ibn Anas, d. 795), **Shafi'i** (al-Shafi'i, d. 820) and **Hanbali** (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, d. 855). The main Shia school is the **Ja'fari** or **Imami** school (from *Imam*, because it follows the Imams of the Prophet's family), named after Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 765). A few jurists from schools that did not last are named where they hold a view, such as Ibn Hazm (d. 1064) of the **Zahiri** ("literalist") school, which kept to the plain wording of the texts. The Qur'an commentator al-Tabari (d. 923) also had a school of his own, the **Jariri** (from his name, Ibn Jarir), which did not last either.
**Suggested teaching plan.** Six sessions of about 90 minutes:

r: The idea, the names, the definitions
Legal nature and the basis for allowing it
The six frameworks; cases and review

blocks.x: Part 1. The word and the idea
1.1 The problem mudarabah solves

Some people have money but not the time, health or skill to run a business. Other people have the skill and energy but no money. Mudarabah joins the two: one side brings the money, the other side brings the work, and they share the profit.

The standard-setter AAOIFI gives this as the reason the contract is allowed: some people are rich but lack business know-how, and others have the know-how but lack money (AAOIFI SS 13, Appendix B). It also notes a second reason: money cannot grow unless it is joined with work, and lending money for a fixed periodic payment would be a debt with *riba* (AAOIFI SS 13, Appendix B).

**Riba** means "increase". In a loan, it is any increase over the amount lent: AAOIFI calls a "fixed or variable increment" on a current account (which is a loan to the bank) "usurious interest" (AAOIFI SS 40, 2/2/1-2/2/2). Islamic law forbids it. Usmani explains the choice this leaves a person with money: if you want to help someone, lend and take back only what you lent; if you want to earn from his business, join it, and then share in its losses as well as its profits (Usmani, p. 18).
1.2 The names
The same contract has three names in the classical books seen for this manual:

i: **Mudarabah.** From the Arabic root *d-r-b* (the three consonants the word is built on), "to strike", used in the phrase *al-darb fi al-ard*, "striking out across the land", that is, travelling for trade. Ibn Qudamah (d. 1223) says this is the name used by the people of Iraq (Ibn Qudamah, *al-Mughni* 5:19). Al-Sarakhsi (d. 1090) explains the name by saying the manager earns his share of the profit through his effort and his work (al-Sarakhsi, *al-Mabsut* 22:17-18).

**Qirad** and **muqaradah.** The name used in the Hijaz (Mecca and Medina). Al-Sarakhsi says the people of Medina call it *muqaradah*, and that this is reported from the caliph Uthman (al-Sarakhsi, *al-Mabsut* 22:17-18). The Muwatta of Malik (Maliki) and the *Minhaj* of al-Nawawi (Shafi'i) use *qirad* as their chapter title.

AAOIFI adds that the contract may be made with the words *mudarabah*, *qirad* or *mu'amalah* ("dealing") (AAOIFI SS 13, 4/1). The Malaysian central bank notes that *muqaradah* and *qirad* mean the same as mudarabah (BNM PD Mudarabah 2015, note 2).

A good class exercise is to read four definitions from four different centuries and find what they share.

A partnership in profit whereby one party provides capital and the other party provides labour (AAOIFI SS 13, clause 2)

A contract under which the capital provider gives capital to be managed by the entrepreneur; profit is shared by an agreed ratio, while financial losses are borne by the capital provider, provided they are not due to the entrepreneur's misconduct, negligence or breach of specified terms (BNM PD Mudarabah 2015, 10.1)

1.5 A first picture

Amina has 100,000 in savings. Bilal is a skilled cloth trader with no capital. Amina gives Bilal the 100,000. They agree that Bilal will trade in cloth and that any profit will be split 60% to Amina and 40% to Bilal. - If Bilal makes a profit of 20,000, Amina gets her 100,000 back plus 12,000; Bilal gets 8,000. - If Bilal makes no profit, Amina gets her 100,000 back and Bilal gets nothing for his work. - If, without any fault of Bilal's, the business loses 10,000, Amina gets 90,000 back. Bilal gets nothing for his work but does not repay the 10,000.

Part 2. Mudarabah in academic terms
2.1 Where mudarabah sits in Islamic contract law

Islamic law sorts contracts into families, and the books do not all place mudarabah in the same one. Ibn Qudamah (Hanbali) places it inside his book on partnership (**shirkah**, "sharing") as its third kind: "a body and wealth share", meaning one partner brings his person (work) and the other brings wealth (*al-Mughni* 5:19). The Muwatta of Malik and the *Minhaj* of al-Nawawi give qirad a book of its own, apart from partnership. AAOIFI's definitions appendix sets out how a mudarabah is distinguished from a partnership (AAOIFI SS 13, App. C). The contract most often compared with it in finance is **musharakah**, where every partner brings money.
Usmani sets out five differences between the two (Usmani, pp. 31-32):

r: The manager only; the investor may not take part
All partners, by their share of capital
The investor only, unless the manager was negligent or dishonest
Limited to the investor's money, unless he allowed borrowing in his name
The investor; the manager earns only from profit when goods are sold

His example, citing al-Nawawi's *Rawdat al-Talibin* 5:125, is sheep that give birth to lambs, which would then be shared by the agreed ratio. Usmani calls this "a minority view" (Usmani, p. 32, note 1).

Two key terms appear in all the modern texts. AAOIFI calls mudarabah "one of the trust-based contracts" (AAOIFI SS 13, 4/4). Bank Negara Malaysia calls it a contract based on a fiduciary relationship, *'aqd al-amanah* ("contract of trust") (BNM PD Mudarabah 2015, 11.1).
2.3 Why it is allowed: the evidence and the debate
Mudarabah is accepted by every school. But the scholars disagree about **what the permission rests on**. Teaching this question well shows learners how Islamic law reasons.
2.3.1 The jurists' admission: strict reasoning would forbid it

Al-Kasani (Hanafi, d. 1191) admits that if one applied strict analogy (*qiyas*) the contract would not be allowed. His reason: it hires a person for an unknown wage, indeed for a wage that may never exist, and for unknown work. "But we left analogy," he says, because of the Qur'an, the Sunnah and consensus (al-Kasani, *Bada'i' al-Sana'i'* 6:79).

**For the teacher:** this is a good moment to explain that Islamic law does not run on analogy alone. Where a practice is approved by the sources and by consensus, the jurists keep it even when analogy points the other way.
2.3.2 Is there a verse of the Qur'an?

r: Cites Qur'an 73:20, which speaks of others travelling in the land seeking the bounty of God, reading it as travel for trade; he says the permission is known by the Sunnah and consensus (*al-Mabsut* 22:18)
Cites the same verse and says the manager is one who travels in the land seeking God's bounty (*Bada'i'* 6:79)
Lists Qur'an 73:20 first among the proofs, read as travel for trade and lawful income (AAOIFI SS 13, App. B)
Reads 73:20 as people travelling for trade and earning, but draws no contract ruling from it (*Jami' al-Bayan*, on 73:20)
Rests qirad on the Prophet's approval of a pre-Islamic practice and on the unbroken practice of Muslims without dispute; the page cites no verse (*al-Muhalla* 7:96, issue 1367)

blocks.x: The word *mudarabah* itself does not appear in the Qur'an. The verse shares its root (*d-r-b*), and the jurists above read it in different ways: as support, or as wording only.
2.3.3 The Prophet and the Companions
Besides the verse, the books cite the practice of the Prophet's time and of his Companions. For Ibn Hazm, this practice is the whole basis (2.3.2).

i: **Before Islam.** Ibn Hazm says qirad existed before Islam, when the Quraysh (the Prophet's tribe in Mecca) gave capital to traders for a share of the profit, and that the Prophet approved it and himself traded with the wealth of Khadijah (later his wife) (*al-Muhalla* 7:96).

**A hadith naming it.** A report in Sunan Ibn Majah lists *muqaradah* among three things that carry blessing. It is graded weak (*da'if*) in the edition used, so it is support rather than proof (Ibn Majah 2289). Mishkat al-Masabih gives the same report; its translator adds a note defining muqaradah as trading with someone's property with profit shared and "any loss falling on the property" (Mishkat 2815).

**Al-'Abbas's conditions.** The Prophet's uncle al-'Abbas is reported to have set conditions on his manager: not to cross the sea with the money, not to go down into a valley, not to buy animals with it; if he did, he would be liable. The report says the Prophet heard of it and approved (al-Sarakhsi, *al-Mabsut* 22:18; al-Kasani, *Bada'i'* 6:79; AAOIFI SS 13, App. B, citing al-Bayhaqi). **Its grade:** al-Bayhaqi records it (*al-Sunan al-Kubra*, Dar al-Kutub al-'Ilmiyya edition, 6:184, nos. 11611-11612) and says only one narrator carries it, Abu al-Jarud Ziyad ibn al-Mundhir, "a weak Kufan" (from Kufa, a city in Iraq). He adds that the hadith critic Yahya ibn Ma'in called him a liar and that the other critics called him weak. Al-Daraqutni, who also records the report, says Abu al-Jarud is weak (as given in the Dorar Encyclopedia of Hadith, dorar.net). The report is therefore weak by its own collector's judgement, and is support rather than proof.

**Hakim ibn Hizam's conditions.** A Companion who set the same kind of conditions and said that if they were broken, the manager would guarantee the money. Ibn Hajar, the compiler of Bulugh al-Maram, notes that al-Daraqutni recorded it and that its narrators are trustworthy (Bulugh al-Maram 1043).

**Umar's sons.** Two sons of the caliph Umar, Abdullah and Ubaydullah, were lent public money in Basra, traded with it and made a profit. Umar ruled the loan had been given only because of who they were. A man sitting with him suggested he treat it as a qirad. Umar did: the treasury took the capital and half the profit, and the sons kept half (Muwatta 1450).
**Uthman.** The caliph Uthman gave money as qirad on condition that the profit be shared (Muwatta 1451).
**An orphan's money.** Ibn Qudamah reports that Umar gave an orphan's wealth as mudarabah, to be traded in Iraq (*al-Mughni* 5:19).

**An early judge.** Ibn Sirin said he knew of the judge Shurayh ruling on mudarabah disputes in only two ways: the manager must prove a calamity to be excused; the investor must prove betrayal, otherwise the manager's oath is enough (Sunan al-Nasa'i 3967, graded *sahih*, "sound", in the edition used).

blocks.x: 2.3.4 The Shia (Ja'fari) reports

The Ja'fari school relies on reports from the Imams of the Prophet's family. Al-Kulayni's *al-Kafi* (compiled before 941) has a chapter titled "Liability for Profit Sharing, Its Profit and Expenses (al-Mudarabah)". In it, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq says the working partner takes his share of the profit but is not liable for loss "unless he violates the instructions of the owner of the assets" (al-Kafi 5, no. 890). The same chapter gives rules on breach, debt as capital, expenses and guarantees, used in Part 3 below.
**For the teacher:** the Sunni and Shia sources reach the same core rule by separate chains of reports: profit is shared, loss falls on the capital, and the manager is liable only for breach.
2.3.5 Consensus

Ibn Qudamah reports that "the people of knowledge agreed on the permissibility of mudaraba in general", citing Ibn al-Mundhir (*al-Mughni* 5:19). AAOIFI repeats this (AAOIFI SS 13, App. B). Ibn Hazm calls it a practice that Muslims followed with certainty and without any disagreement (*al-Muhalla* 7:96).
2.4 The building blocks (pillars)
The jurists analyse a contract into its "pillars" (*arkan*), the parts without which it does not exist. They do not all count the same pillars.

i: **Al-Kasani (Hanafi):** "As for the pillar of the contract, it is offer and acceptance" (*Bada'i'* 6:79). He then treats the parties, the capital and the profit as conditions of that pillar, not as pillars: some conditions relate to the two parties, some to the capital and some to the profit (*Bada'i'* 6:81).

**A Shafi'i commentary:** "Its pillars are six: the two contracting parties, work, profit, capital and the formula" (the formula is the offer and acceptance; the two parties count as two pillars) (*Mukhtasar Tuhfat al-Muhtaj* 2:381, a modern abridgement, prepared by Mustafa ibn Sumayt, of the commentary *Tuhfat al-Muhtaj* by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami on al-Nawawi's *Minhaj*; he is a different person from the Ibn Hajar who compiled *Bulugh al-Maram*).

**A modern comparative study** reports that the majority, the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, count five pillars (the two parties, the formula, the capital, the work and the profit), and that the Hanafis count one, the formula (Fahd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Dahmash, "al-Mudarabah: dirasah muqaranah li-l-shurut al-mufsidah li-l-'aqd wa-tatbiqatuha al-qada'iyyah", *Majallat al-Dirasat al-'Arabiyyah*, Minya University, vol. 51, no. 1, January 2025, pp. 247-276, abstract). This manual does not quote the Maliki and Hanbali books themselves on this point.

**The modern standards** set the contract out in parts. Bank Negara Malaysia groups them as the "components of mudarabah": the contracting parties, offer and acceptance, management, capital, profit and loss (BNM 12-17).

Part 3. The rules, with every school's position

This part takes the contract apart one question at a time. Each section first gives what the sources agree on, then any disagreement, with its holders. A summary table of all disagreements is at 3.14.
3.1 The capital: cash only, or goods too?

**Agreed:** cash (in the classical books, gold and silver coin: dirhams and dinars) may be the capital. Ibn Qudamah writes that there is "no disagreement" that dirhams and dinars may serve as capital in a partnership (*al-Mughni* 5:12).
**Disputed:** may the investor hand over goods (Arabic *'urud*, trade goods or other non-cash assets) as the capital?

**The reports conflict.** Ibn Qudamah knows of no one who disagrees, while the later Hanbali manual records a second narration from Ahmad that allows it, and Ibn al-Qayyim is reported as arguing for it. This manual does not settle the question.

**A debt owed by someone else.** Al-Kasani (Hanafi) allows the investor to say "collect what so-and-so owes me and work with it as mudarabah": the mudarabah then attaches to the money once received, so the capital is cash, not a debt (*Bada'i'* 6:83, as quoted in *Fiqh al-Mu'amalat*). 3.8 What the manager may and may not do

**In an unrestricted mudarabah** the manager may do what traders in his field normally do. AAOIFI lists examples: choose fields and markets, do the work himself or appoint someone for part of it, keep the funds with a trustworthy custodian, buy and sell on credit (AAOIFI SS 13, 9/1).

**Things he may not do** without the investor's consent: lend, give gifts or charity from the funds, or waive a right of the business (AAOIFI SS 13, 9/6); sell below or buy above market price without a clear business reason (9/5). Malik says he may not give any of the money away, even to a beggar (Muwatta 1460).

**Work he must do himself.** The manager must do the work any similar manager would do by custom. If he hires someone for that work, he pays from his own pocket; he may hire at the business's cost only for work outside the custom of his role (AAOIFI SS 13, 9/4). 4.1 Where it fits in a modern bank

Usmani calls musharakah and mudarabah "the real and ideal instruments of financing" in Islamic law, because money given on these terms must turn into real assets, and profit comes from selling them (Usmani, p. 12). He also says that in the current economic set-up there are "certain practical difficulties" in using them in some areas of financing, which is why scholars have allowed murabahah (a cost-plus sale) under conditions, as a step on the way and not an ideal instrument (Usmani, p. 72).
A bank can stand on either side of a mudarabah:

r: Mudarabah financing of a business, project or trade deal (4.2)
Investment accounts, also called profit-sharing investment accounts (4.3)

blocks.x: When it does both at once, it is a **multi-tier** mudarabah: depositors invest with the bank as manager, and the bank invests those funds with businesses as investor. BNM describes this: in the first tier the investor and manager agree one ratio; in the second tier the first manager, now acting as investor, agrees another ratio with a new manager (BNM 16.11). BNM also allows a manager, with the investor's consent, to place the funds with another manager (BNM 14.4).
4.2 The bank as investor: financing
Usmani sets out four principles for any bank finance on these terms (Usmani, pp. 37-38):

i: Financing is not lending money. It is joining the business.
The financier shares in loss, up to what he financed.
Profit ratios are agreed freely, but "the partner who has expressly excluded himself from the responsibility of work for the business cannot claim more than the ratio of his investment".
Loss is always shared exactly by capital.

blocks.x: **Uses Usmani describes:**

i: **A whole project.** The bank pays for the project and the client runs it: the bank is investor, the client manager (Usmani, p. 38).

**A single import.** An importer's bank usually opens a *letter of credit* (L/C), its undertaking to pay the foreign supplier. If the L/C is opened "without any margin" (no deposit from the importer), mudarabah can be used; if it is opened "with some margin", musharakah or the combination of 3.10 (Usmani, p. 42).

**Exports.** Usmani says musharakah "will be even easier" here, and that the financier may use musharakah or mudarabah. The exporter already has an order at a known price, so the profit can be estimated. The financier may require the exporter to ship in full conformity with the L/C; if "discrepancies" are found in the documents, the exporter alone is responsible, while other losses are shared (Usmani, pp. 42-43).

blocks.x: **Project finance, as the IFSB describes it.** A bank advances funds to a construction company as manager. The company is paid in stages by its own customer. The bank can require those stage payments to go into a "repayment account" at the bank, from which the manager may not withdraw without the bank's permission. The bank shares the profit of the project but bears 100% of any loss (IFSB-2, para. 188(c)).

**Exit.** The IFSB asks banks to set out in advance how they will leave a mudarabah or musharakah investment, including extension and redemption terms, "subject to the approval of the institution's Shari'ah Board" (IFSB-1, Principle 3.3). BNM allows the manager to promise (*wa'd*) to buy the mudarabah assets at market value, fair value or a price agreed at the time of purchase (BNM 21.1-21.2). Note what is not allowed: a promise that works as a guarantee of the capital (3.6).
**A worked example for class** *(illustration made for this manual)*:

A bank gives a trading company 1,000,000 as mudarabah for one year, profit 30% to the bank and 70% to the company. - **Year profit 200,000.** Bank: 60,000. Company: 140,000. Bank gets its 1,000,000 back. - **No profit.** Bank gets 1,000,000 back. Company earns nothing for its year of work. - **Loss of 150,000, no fault.** Bank gets 850,000 back and bears the loss. Company earns nothing. - **Loss of 150,000 because the company broke a restriction** (it traded in goods the contract excluded). The company must make good the 150,000 (3.5, 3.8).
4.3 The bank as manager: investment accounts
Here the depositors are the investors and the bank is the manager.
**Two kinds of account** (AAOIFI SS 40, 2/1):

i: **Unrestricted investment accounts:** the bank may invest the money as it sees fit.
**Restricted investment accounts:** the money goes into a named project or programme.

blocks.x: **How they differ from a current account.** A current account is a loan to the bank: the bank guarantees repayment and may pay no fixed or variable increase, because that would be riba. An investment account is not guaranteed; the bank only distributes the profit actually earned (AAOIFI SS 40, 2/2/1-2/2/2).
**Profit to the depositors: the rules of AAOIFI SS 40.**

i: No profit before the capital is protected. A payout before that is an advance, not profit (3/1/1).
Profit is known only after actual liquidation (assets sold) or constructive liquidation (assets valued by experts, debts valued with provisions) (3/1/2/1).
Costs the bank must bear as manager, such as its investment department, may not be charged to depositors (3/1/2/2).
Losses of one operation may be covered by profits of others in the same period; a loss of one period may not be covered by profit of another, except through reserves (3/2/1).
Profit among depositors may be shared by a **points method**: amount of money multiplied by the time it stayed invested (5/1).
The bank may announce an **expected rate of return**, but it is not binding; final payout follows the actual profit (5/2).
Advances on account are allowed and corrected after liquidation (5/3).
If the bank, as manager, gives up part of its own profit share to depositors after the accounts are drawn up, it must disclose this (5/6).

He says the classical books give no express answer, and that his suggestion "needs further consideration and research by the experts of Islamic jurisprudence" (Usmani, pp. 47-48). He reports two objections and answers each:

r: "Some contemporary scholars" reject the method as "just a conjectural method" that does not reflect the profit each partner really earned, since a partner may have had little money in the pool when large profits were made (pp. 48-49)

Once a pool exists, its profits are earned by all participants, whether or not their own money was used in a given deal; the Hanafi school does not require the partners' money to be mixed (pp. 49-50, citing al-Kasani, *Bada'i'* 6:54, 60)
The capital of each partner is unknown when the contract is made. Usmani reports, quoting al-Kasani, that knowing the capital is a condition "according to Imam Shafi'i" (p. 50)
For the Hanafis it is not a condition; what matters is that the profit is not uncertain at distribution, which daily products achieve (pp. 50-51, citing al-Kasani, *Bada'i'* 6:63)

blocks.x: He adds that without daily products, no one could deposit or withdraw except on fixed start dates, an arrangement he calls "totally impracticable on the deposits side of the banks" (pp. 51-52).
4.4 Smoothing and reserves

Depositors compare a bank's payout with its competitors' and may leave if it is lower. Banks therefore try to keep payouts steady. The IFSB calls the pressure **displaced commercial risk**: a bank under market pressure may pay depositors more than the assets earned, for example by giving up part or all of its own manager's share (IFSB-1, para. 104). The IFSB adds a limit: this does not extend to covering an overall loss of the depositors by moving profit from shareholders, which it says Shari'ah rules do not permit (IFSB-2, para. 76).
Two reserves are used (IFSB-2, para. 80; IFSB-1, paras. 105-106):

r: Gross income of the mudarabah, **before** the bank's manager share
To smooth returns paid to depositors and shareholders
The depositors' income, **after** the bank's manager share
To meet future losses on investments funded by depositors

blocks.x: AAOIFI fixes the order: reserves for bad debts and for rate of return come out of gross profit; the reserve for investment risks comes out after the manager's share (AAOIFI SS 40, 3/1/2/3). BNM: a reserve may be made only from profit, and only the investor's part of it may be used to make up lost capital, so that the reserve does not become a capital guarantee by the manager (BNM 16.23-16.25 and note 6). The IFSB sets out the practice in a separate guidance note on smoothing (IFSB GN-3, December 2010).
**For the teacher:** reserves are where practice comes closest to the forbidden guarantee. Ask learners: at what point does a smoothed, "expected" return become a fixed return in substance?
4.5 A critical view
Islamic finance has its own critics from within, and a teacher should present them alongside the industry's view.

**Mahmoud El-Gamal**, an economist at Rice University, argues that "investment-account holders have neither the protection of being creditors of the Islamic financial institution" nor the protection of being "equity holders with representation on those institutions' boards of directors" (El-Gamal 2007, p. 212). He notes that one industry leader, Sheikh Kamel, prefers to call customers "partner" rather than "customer or depositor" (p. 211). He sees a risk that "account holders will withdraw their funds for fear of excessive risk taking" (p. 212). His proposed remedy is mutualisation, making depositors the owners of the institution; he says "the mutuality structure ... would solve one of the most difficult regulatory and governance issues raised by these institutions" (p. 212). More widely, he writes that "Shari'a arbitrage is a particular form of regulatory arbitrage", in which lawyers offer clients "a reengineered version" of conventional products (El-Gamal, "Limits and Dangers of Shari'a Arbitrage").

**The other side.** The standard-setters treat the investment account as a real mudarabah with real rules. AAOIFI requires that no profit be paid before capital is protected and that expected rates are not binding (SS 40, 3/1/1, 5/2). The IFSB recognises depositors' rights to monitor their investments and requires that smoothing be transparent (IFSB-30, Principles 14 and 15). Usmani, while preferring mudarabah and musharakah, accepts other contracts in a transition, under strict conditions (Usmani, pp. 12, 72).

6.1 Case studies
*All five cases are illustrations made for this manual.*

**Case 1: The guaranteed partner.** An investor gives 500,000 to a builder as mudarabah, profit 50/50. The contract adds: "The builder guarantees return of the capital in all cases." The project loses 100,000 through a market fall; the builder did nothing wrong.
*Questions:* Is the guarantee valid? What does the investor receive?

*Discussion points:* The manager may not guarantee the capital (3.6). Malik: the stipulation of guarantees in qirad is void, and the profit is shared as if there were no guarantee (Muwatta 1455); the builder owes nothing for the loss. The Ja'fari report in al-Kafi 5, no. 886 takes a different route: "One who holds a merchant responsible he can only have his capital and has no share in the profit" (in this manual's words, the investor is treated like a lender). AAOIFI: guarantees can be enforced only for misconduct, negligence or breach (SS 13, 6). Ask learners to compare the classical outcomes.
**Case 2: The restricted trader.** An investor gives 200,000 for trade "in textiles only, in Karachi only". The manager makes a profitable trade in electronics in Lahore.
*Questions:* Who gets the profit? Who would have borne a loss?

*Discussion points:* Two Ja'fari reports: if the manager goes beyond the place set, he is liable for loss, but profit is shared (al-Kafi 5, nos. 884-885). Al-Kasani on restrictions that are expressly forbidden (*Bada'i'* 6:99). Hakim ibn Hizam's conditions (Bulugh al-Maram 1043). On the profit, compare the holders in 3.8: shared as agreed, the investor's choice (Malik), to the investor (Imam Ahmad), or given in charity. On liability, Ali's saying and Ibn Qudamah's answer (*al-Mughni* 5:39).
**Case 3: The fixed-term fund.** A bank raises money for a five-year mudarabah fund and wants investors locked in for three years.
*Questions:* Which schools allow a term? Is a lock-in allowed?
*Discussion points:* On a fixed term: Hanafi yes; Hanbali two narrations; Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hazm no (3.9). On the lock-in: Usmani's own view (p. 35), AAOIFI SS 13, 4/3/2, BNM 11.2(c).

**Case 4: The smoothed account.** A bank's investment pool earns 2% this year. Competitors pay 4%. The bank pays depositors 4% by drawing on its profit equalisation reserve and giving up its own manager share.
*Questions:* Is this allowed? What must the bank disclose? What does it mean for capital?
*Discussion points:* SS 40, 3/1/2/3 and 5/6; IFSB-1, paras. 104-105; IFSB-2, paras. 76-80; El-Gamal's critique (4.5).
**Case 5: The debt rollover.** A trader owes a merchant 50,000 and cannot pay. The merchant says: "Keep it as mudarabah capital and give me half your profit."

*Discussion points:* Malik (Muwatta 1453, 1463), al-Kafi 5, no. 887, Ibn Qudamah (*al-Mughni* 5:190, as quoted in *Fiqh al-Mu'amalat*), AAOIFI SS 13, 7/3, BNM 15.7. Why most sources see riba in it. The other side: the second narration from Ahmad and Ibn al-Qayyim, as reported (3.2).
6.2 Review questions (with answers)

i: **Name the two parties in Arabic and English.** *Rabb al-mal*, the investor; *mudarib*, the manager.
**Name two other words for mudarabah.** *Qirad* and *muqaradah* (also *mu'amalah* in AAOIFI SS 13, 4/1).
**Who bears a money loss?** The investor, up to his capital. The manager loses his work.
**Name the three faults that make the manager liable.** Misconduct (*ta'addi*), negligence (*taqsir*), breach of terms (*mukhalafat al-shurut*).
**Is "the manager gets 10% of the capital as profit" valid?** No: profit must be a share of actual profit, not of capital.

**Can the manager draw a salary?** No, apart from his profit share; a separate fee is allowed only for work outside his role (AAOIFI SS 13, 8/2). Expenses are a separate question: AAOIFI allows agreed or customary living expenses and travel expenses (SS 13, 9/7), and the schools differ (3.7).
**Which schools allow a fixed term?** The Hanafis, and the Hanbalis in one of two narrations. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Hazm do not.

**What does al-Kasani say strict analogy would conclude, and why was it set aside?** That mudarabah is invalid (unknown wage, unknown work); it was set aside because of the Qur'an, Sunnah and consensus (*Bada'i'* 6:79).
**What happens if a manager adds his own money?** It becomes mudarabah and musharakah combined; he takes profit for his money, then the mudarabah split applies; loss follows capital.
**What is the difference between PER and IRR?** PER is taken before the manager's share, to smooth returns; IRR is taken from depositors' income after the manager's share, to meet future losses.
**What risk weight does IFSB-23 give a mudarabah investment in a commercial enterprise?** 250%; 400% if it is a short-term unlisted equity exposure.

**When does FAS 51 replace FAS 3?** For financial statements beginning on or after 1 January 2027; an institution may choose to apply it only to transactions made on or after that date (FAS 51, paras. 74-76).
